props.title: Borsalino
props.initialSlug: Two gangsters rise to power in 1930s Marseille

sections.content: Borsalino (1970) represents the pinnacle of European gangster chic, pairing French megastars Alain Delon and Jean-Paul Belmondo at the height of their powers. Set in 1930s Marseille, the film captures the swagger and style of French crime cinema while paying homage to American gangster classics like The Public Enemy (1931) and Little Caesar (1931). Director Jacques Deray crafts a sun-drenched Mediterranean noir that influenced later films like The Godfather (1972) with its blend of fashion, violence, and criminal empire building.

sections.content: The film's massive success spawned numerous European crime films in the 1970s trying to capture its blend of period detail and contemporary cool. The Marseille Contract (1974) and The Italian Connection (1972) borrowed heavily from Borsalino's template. The film's influence extends to modern neo-noirs like Drive (2011), which references its mix of brutality and refinement. SUBHEAD: The French Connection - Style and Crime

Borsalino's impact on fashion and popular culture was immediate - the titular Borsalino fedora became a must-have accessory. This intersection of crime and style influenced films like Casino (1995) and Goodfellas (1990), where the gangsters' fashion choices reflect their rise in criminal society. The film's Mediterranean setting and sun-bleached cinematography by Jean-Jacques Tarbès created a template for later Euro-crime films like The Connection (2014).
